extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / wartime public (readers of AP/Reuters-era dispatches)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing concise news dispatches about wartime military actions, combining official communiqués, reconnaissance reports, enemy broadcasts, and eyewitness/command quotes to inform the public. Emphasizes attribution, verification caveats, and operational detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of claims to named sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute every report or claim to its origin: e.g., 'the Berlin radio said', 'the Air Ministry announced', 'reported by the Associated Press', 'British sources said'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always name the source of a claim (enemy radio broadcasts, ministry statements, reconnaissance, Reuters/AP, British sources). Use verbs like 'said', 'reported', 'announced' to make clear who is claiming the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and treat enemy broadcasts/propaganda as unverified
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting enemy or adversary radio/press claims, clearly flag them: e.g., the copy notes 'The Berlin radio said' and also uses phrasing like 'must be regarded as propaganda rather than as a military report.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present enemy claims as fact. Mark such material as reported by the adversary and, where appropriate, explicitly call it propaganda or unverified until corroborated by independent or official sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present casualty and damage figures with caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures in the dispatch are given alongside qualifiers: 'killed forty-two children and five teachers', 'figures on plane losses', 'American losses were not announced' and 'no details'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish numbers but include context about their source and reliability; if officials have not announced figures or sources conflict, state that explicitly. Avoid definitive totals when data remain provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official communiqués and reconnaissance as primary verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites 'official reports', 'Air Ministry announced', and 'pictures taken by reconnaissance planes pieced together' as bases for verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize official communiqués, reconnaissance photos, and confirmed ministry statements as verification. Note when such evidence has been used to corroborate or contradict claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide precise geographic and temporal context
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports supply dates, times and locations: e.g., 'London, Feb. 10', '4:25 P.M. (Guadalcanal time)', 'home counties', 'Lorient', 'Kendari Harbor'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify dates, times (with time zone/context) and exact place names to orient readers. When relevant, include distances, directional cues or theater identifiers (e.g., 'South Pacific', 'home counties').

rubrics_metrics.name: Include technical and operational military details
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatches note aircraft types, ordnance and technical specifics: e.g., 'a low-wing monoplane with a crew of two', 'top speed is estimated at 18,000 feet', 'twin-engine ME-201A-1', 'carrying 2,200 pounds of bombs', 'self-sealing fuel tanks holding 550 gallons'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply technical details (vehicle/aircraft type, armament, tonnage, altitude, composition of forces) where they aid reader understanding of scale and capability, and attribute technical claims to an identified source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report conflicting accounts and official denials
rubrics_metrics.description: The copy juxtaposes opposing claims (enemy broadcasts vs Allied communiqués): e.g., Japanese communiqués vs MacArthur's 'It is a complete fabrication', British reports vs Berlin radio statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sources disagree, present each account with its attribution and, where possible, provide counter-evidence or official denials so readers can see the contradiction and the basis for acceptance or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess strategic significance through authoritative quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: The article includes interpretation from officials: e.g., 'Seizure of Guadalcanal has an important part in plan', Captain Browning: 'Guadalcanal was never of any importance except for its airfield and as a jumping-off point.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include quotations or succinct analysis from commanders, officials or experts to explain the strategic meaning of events, but attribute those judgments and distinguish them from factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cautious, non-sensational language when evidence is incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: The copy frequently uses hedging and qualifiers ('probably', 'no details', 'appeared', 'claimed') and avoids asserting unverified outcomes as facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measured wording and hedges when information is partial. Avoid definitive or sensational claims until corroborated; explicitly note areas of uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include eyewitness or on-scene color while maintaining factual core
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatches add on-the-ground color and quotes (e.g., descriptions of anti-aircraft fire, people hurrying home, 'the all clear sounded a short time later') alongside core facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eyewitness detail to bring reports to life, but keep it secondary to verified facts and clearly mark anecdotal or eyewitness material as such.
